resources.string: How lymph returns to the blood
One route through the thoracic duct. Tracers show direction, not speed or personal lymphatic function.
Water and some small molecules filter from blood capillaries into spaces between cells. Blood cells generally stay within the vessel.
Tissue fluid can enter a blind-ended lymphatic capillary between flap-like edges of neighboring endothelial cells. Once inside it is called lymph.
Segments of collecting vessels can fill and contract. Valves open and close with local pressure changes and help limit backflow.
Lymph enters through afferent vessels, flows through the sinuses, and leaves through an efferent vessel. Immune cells can sample some of the material it carries.
Lymph from most of the body enters the thoracic duct and usually returns near the junction of the left internal jugular and subclavian veins.
One example of a T-cell-dependent antibody response. Timing, cell counts, and immune test results are not modeled.
Part of an antigen can bind to a matching receptor on a B cell. Different B cells recognize different antigen features.
A B cell can process an antigen and display a fragment. A helper T cell that recognizes the displayed fragment provides additional signals in this type of response.
B cells receiving appropriate signals can multiply, expanding the population that recognizes that antigen feature.
Plasma and memory B cells form
Some descendants become antibody-secreting plasma cells. Others can become memory B cells for a later encounter with the same antigen feature.
Plasma cells secrete antibodies. Antibodies bind matching antigen features and can neutralize or mark targets in different contexts.
